item.title: God is not responsible, and these two are responsible for his death
item.description: a guest-post by Stephen Kershnar and Nathan Bray
item.content:encoded:
The following is a guest post by and Nathan Bray. Nathan is a doctoral student in philosophy at the University of St. Andrews, a university that rejected me for undergrad and caused me to hate all of Scotland. Kershnar is, besides Peter Singer, the most controversial philosopher in the world. In this post, they raise an interesting challenge totheism, at the cutting edge of ethics, philosophy of religion, and action theory. Enjoy!

Subscribe now

God is not morally responsible. This is a problem for theism.

Let us first set out a few notions. First, God is the greatest possible being.

Second, in this context, greatness consists of, and only of, intrinsic value. There is no greatness simpliciter. When ranking Bach’s songs, integers, and football players, they do not share a type of greatness independent of a relevant property. Extrinsic value is only derivative value. Extrinsically valuable things are valuable because they bring about intrinsically valuable things. If this is correct, then if God is the greatest possible being, then he is maximally intrinsically valuable. If God is maximally intrinsically valuable, then – we claim – he is essentially omnibenevolent (that is, all-good).

Third, responsibility is a basic property. We cannot reduce it to more basic properties. It is similar to the good or the right. In terms of synonyms, we can think about responsibility as being apt for praise or blame, or – alternatively – basically deserving praise or blame.

Given these assumptions, God is not significantly responsible. Roughly, a person is significantly responsible just in case he can be responsible for doing good and he can be responsible for doing evil. If God is the greatest possible being, then his psychology is (essentially and maximally) all-good. If God’s psychology is all-good, then he cannot have an evil attitude. If God cannot have an evil attitude, then nothing can motivate him to do evil. If nothing can motivate God to do evil, then he can’t decide to do evil. If God can’t decide to do evil, then he can’t do evil. If God can’t do something, then he can’t be responsible for not doing it. Hence, God is not responsible for not doing evil. If trying to do evil is itself evil, then God can’t do that either.

The following table summarizes this argument.

A theist might still think that God can be insignificantly responsible. The theist might say God can be responsible for doing good but not for avoiding evil. More specifically, he can be praiseworthy even if he can’t be blameworthy. For example, he might be praiseworthy for creating the best possible world or for answering someone’s prayer.

Contra the theist, God is not insignificantly responsible for two reasons: his psychology compels his acts, and he is similar to an instantly created being, and such a being is not responsible. Let’s consider these reasons.

First, God’s psychology compels his actions. Consider this case.

Case #1: Kleptomaniac

Al is a kleptomaniac. Specifically, he has an ineliminable and extremely strong desire to steal. He authorizes this desire. Specifically, he makes the desire an authentic part of his psychology by endorsing it or identifying with it. Al’s desire to steal leads him to his deciding to steal, and this decision leads to his stealing. He is the source of his decision in the sense that if he were to decide not to steal, he wouldn’t steal. He is also the source of his decision in that his desire inclines him to steal, but does not necessitate his doing so.

Intuitively, Al is not responsible – specifically, blameworthy – for stealing.

Next, consider this case.

Case #2: Kleptophobe

Bob is identical to Al, except that Bob has an ineliminable and extremely strong desire not to steal. Bob authorizes this desire. His desire leads him to his deciding not to steal, and his decision leads to his not stealing.

If Al is not responsible for stealing, then Bob is not responsible for not stealing. They differ only in the content of a single desire. This difference is not a responsibility-maker. The difference in content does not make one person have more control over his thoughts or acts than the second person.

Next, consider this case.

Case #3: Klepto-Correct

Carl is identical to Al and Bob, except that Carl has an ineliminable and extremely strong desire to steal when, and only when, he is morally required to do so (for example, when necessary to save a starving child’s life). Carl authorizes this desire.

If Bob is not responsible for not stealing, then Carl is not responsible for stealing when, and only when, he is morally required to do so. Bob and Carl are similar responsibility-wise.

Last, consider this case.

Case #4: Divine Klepto-Correct

God’s desire is similar to Carl’s desire, except that God’s desire regarding stealing is infinitely strong and no other desire opposes it. God authorizes this desire.

If Carl is not responsible for stealing when, and only when, he is morally required to do so, then God is not responsible for stealing when, and only when, he is morally required to do so. Their desires are similar. Because God has his psychology essentially, he has no more control over it than does Carl. Nor can one authorize a desire in a way that is independent of the authorizer’s psychology. A person cannot do so any more than he can step outside of what constitutes him, for example, a body, brain, or soul. A parallel thing is true if a belief or value motivates God rather than a desire.

The following table summarizes the argument.

Subscribe now

In short, God is not responsible for his psychology, and his psychology compels his action in the same way the kleptomaniac’s desire compels his action. This is true even if God has agent-causal power or is the sole source of his action. God is the sole source of his action just in case he thinks and acts independently of anything extrinsic to him and does not think or act from a brute – that is, random or arbitrary – preference.

Consider the second reason that God is not responsible: he is similar to an instantly created being. Consider this case.

Case #5: Manipulation

Symbionese Liberation Army members manipulate Patty Hearst. Specifically, they create a psychology in her. If Patty acts immediately after being manipulated, she is not responsible for her act.

Let’s call manipulated the person, “Patty #1.” She is not responsible because the manipulator involuntarily reshaped her psychology and – in so doing – made her authorize it. Patty #1 is not responsible for her act because she cannot step outside her psychology and act contrary to it. She cannot step outside her psychology any more than she can step outside of who she is – for example, a body, brain, or soul – and change that thing.

On one theory, a person is responsible for a manipulated psychology only if she had sufficient time to revise her psychology or to affect whether and how her actions flow from it. Depending on the account, sufficient time is a matter of what is fair, reasonable, or responsibility-grounding. Ignore the fact that these conditions beg the question regarding responsibility. Patty #1 did not have sufficient time to revise her psychology.

Next, reflect on this case.

Case #6: Instant Creation

God creates Patty Hearst’s doppelganger ex nihilo. Because the creator created her ex nihilo, the doppelganger has a new psychology. If Patty acts immediately after being created, she is not responsible for her act.

Let’s call the instantly created person, “Patty #2.” If Patty #1 is neither responsible for her newly manipulated psychology nor for what she does immediately after manipulation, then neither is Patty #2. Patty #2 is not responsible for her act because she also cannot step outside her psychology and act contrary to it.

Next, consider this case.

Case #7: Essential Property

A second Patty Hearst doppelganger has her psychology essentially.

Let us call this doppelganger, “Patty #3.” If Patty #2 is not responsible, then neither is Patty #3. Patty #3 has no more control over her psychology – or an act that flows from it – than does Patty #2.

God is similar responsibility-wise to Patty #3. As a result, if Patty #3 is not responsible, then neither is God. God didn’t control his psychology – or an act that flows from it – any more than did Patty #3.

This table summarizes the argument.

What makes this argument go is that in the manipulation, instant creation, and essential psychology cases, the agent cannot step outside her psychology and, so, meaningfully control her psychology or what flows from it. As a result, she is not responsible for an act that flows from psychology. The agent can authorize her psychology – perhaps by endorsing it or by identifying with it – but she has no more control over the authorization than she has over any other act or attitude.

The Judeo-Christian theist cannot accept this result. First, this type of theist thinks we should worship God. One person worships a second just in case the first expresses gratitude to the second. The first’s worship is correct just in case the second merits gratitude. Gratitude entails responsibility. One person can be correctly grateful to a second person only if the second is morally responsible for trying to benefit the first. Appreciation differs from gratitude. For example, a person can appreciate his newborn son, the land he grew up on, or his pet Komodo dragon, but he can’t – correctly – be grateful to them because they aren’t responsible for trying to benefit him.

In addition, theists often claim that the free-will defense is correct. That is, the value of responsible creatures is so great that it justifies God allowing and creating evil. Specifically, it justifies his allowing moral evil – for example, murder – and creating natural evil – for example, cancer. On this theory, responsibility is a great-maker or a feature of a great-maker, for example, soul-building. So important is responsibility that it even justifies God’s sending some people to heaven and some to hell. It is an odd view that responsibility is incredibly important for people but not for God. By analogy – paraphrasing Robert Nozick – it would be odd to say that we should be Kantians regarding human beings but utilitarians regarding God.

One objector might claim that God is responsible because source incompatibilism is true. On this objection, a person is responsible to the extent to which he is the source of his actions. Because God is the sole source of his actions, the objector claims, he is maximally responsible. The problem is that source incompatibilism is false. Compulsion undermines responsibility regardless of whether a person is the sole source of his action.

A second objector might concede that God is not responsible, but claim that – in God – responsibility is not a great-making property. The objector argues that the defining feature of the greatest possible being is that he is essentially omnibenevolent and that any property that contradicts essential omnibenevolence is not a great-maker. The problem with this objection is that that it contradicts how we see God. Denying that God is responsible makes him robot-like. This contradicts our intuitive picture of the greatest possible being. No one wants a Stepford God. In addition, we intuitively think that a person who is responsible for making or maintaining his goodness is better than one who doesn’t do these things. It is strange that this is not also true for God.

— Stephen Kershnar and Nathan Bray

item.title: Baháʼí Philosophy of Religion w/ Joshua Hall
item.content:encoded:
This past week I have been furiously rabbit-holing Baháʼí, a new-ish religion founded by Bahā’ullāh—the 19th Century revelator, Persian prophet, and Manifestation of God.

Baháʼí teaches the unity of religions, human equality, and a unique flavour of globalist politics. It also has a cool and possibly Hume-proof1 miracle in its early history—a real-life analogue of Leslie’s firing squad—which the Baháʼís, a humble people, don’t bang on about as much as Christians or Muslims would if the same event were part of their histories.

To help me get a handle on Baháʼí philosophy and theology, I asked Joshua Hall— cradle Baháʼí, historian of philosophy, and polyglot—to walk me through the religion of and .

Joshua did his MPhil in Islamic Studies and History at Oxford, and is now dissertating on Avicenna at UCLA. To my knowledge, he is the only living Baháʼí doing analytic philosophy of religion. (For a list of his translations, as well as his 84-page paper on the attributes of God in Baháʼí, see this website here.)

In our conversation, we discussed, among other topics, Baháʼí history, Baháʼí politics, classical theism, soteriology, animal ethics, the miracle of the Bab, the limits of religious pluralism, common objections to Baháʼí, and Joshua’s personal pitch for taking the faith seriously as Something-That-Might-Be-True.

Enjoy!

item.title: "Wake up, the new Knives Out is over"
item.content:encoded:
CONTAINS MAJOR SPOILERS: if you have not seen the film, *do not* read this review; it contains the name(s) of the culprit(s), part of the murder method, and other spoilers besides.

How many miligrams of pentobarbital must you inject before watching Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery?

The script was something else. Early on, the screenwriters must’ve put their heads together, debated the most religiousy name for Jesus and the most Jesusy name for congregants, and resolved on ‘Christ’ and ‘flock’. The product was basically,

MONSIGNOR WICKS: By the venegful power of Christ, I am shepherding my flock away from the feminist Marxist whores!

FATHER JUD: Respectfully Monsignor Wicks, you should be shepherding your flock towards the loving heart of Christ.

WICKS: Christ wants me to shepherd his flock away from the feminist Marxist whores. Christ! Are you trying to steal my flock away from me? I masturbated thirty-six times this morning to the vengeful body of Christ!

JUD: Christ no! [*sheepishly*] Sorry for saying ‘Christ’. I’m only trying to shepherd your flock back to Christ!

The one good thing about the film was Josh O’Connor—his performance single-handedly saved it; in spite of his lines (“young, dumb, and full of Christ” [!]), he seemed like a real Catholic priest, the sort you might meet in real life. But excluding Bishop Langstrom, who was also great, the other Catholics just did not sound like real Catholics; through no fault of the actors, their portrayals felt like what I expect I’d see if I watched one of those early 20th Century films about Oriental Chinamen from the Orient—whoever had the job of immersing themselves in Catholic culture, including online, right-wing, tradcath culture, to find out how they talk, did not do that job, and result is what you’d expect.

Benoit Blanc seemed different, and worse. In the other movies his schtick was stylish and likeable, but in this film he is a Reddit-tier neckbeard atheist with a weird haircut who says cringe-maxxing things like “I kneel at the altar of the rational”; their efforts to make him seem like less of a fedora-wearer—having lights shine through the stain glass window when he stops being so aggro about religion—were on the nose and pandering.

The strangest choice plot-wise was that the person whodunnit is the person you’re meant to suspect within the first fifteen minutes, and are given no reason to exclude for the rest of the more than two-hour film. Like, the killer is the evil-looking woman telling a manifestly made up story about about Monsignor Wick’s mother being a demon-possessed harlot whore who smashes up a church in the Hellish light of a bright red moon because she is a harlot whore who is possessed by demons, a story that involves two people randomly dying. From there on out, we are given no reason to exclude Martha, and lo and behold, she’s the killer.

It was still a murder mystery, I guess. Even if we were meant to think the whole way through that Martha did it, it was still a mystery how she did it (the only bit I guessed was that the knife handle was pre-attatched to the priestly vestments, but I guessed wrongly that that knife would be a recoily one—like in the first movies—that shot out of the handle when triggered by a remote); and because the ‘surely it’s Martha’ priming was so overt from the outset, I excluded her as the killer because it’s never the person you’re meant to suspect.

So, fair play to them, but I take it the reason why most murder mysteries don’t make it the character you most suspect is that is makes the resolution a let down.

item.title: The Case For Prayer, For People Who Don't Yet Believe
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday the great a guest essay by the (I’m sure) great Nir Eyal, titled “The Case For Prayer, Even If You’re An Atheist”.

When I clicked on the piece, my mind turned to a paper by the the great Tim Mawson—my philosophy professor last term at Oxford, great in both wisdom and stature—called, provocatively, “Praying to stop being an atheist”.

According to Mawson, “atheists who think that the issue of God’s existence or non-existence is an important one; who assign anything greater than a negligible probability to God’s existence; and who are not in possession of a plausible argument for scepticism about the truth-directedness of the practice of uttering such prayers in their own cases are under a prima facie epistemic obligation to pray to God that He stop them being atheists.”

Subscribe now

Why, you ask? Here is Mawson’s pitch in a nutshell:

I suggest that the person who prays that God help him or her to believe in Him is as reasonable as someone who finds himself or herself shouting ‘Is anyone there?’ in a darkened room about which he or she has various reasonable prior beliefs. This is a room about the other occupier of which, if any, he or she has heard some controversy. Some say that in this room there is a wise old man in an ongoing relationship with whom they have found great personal satisfaction whenever they have entered the room and spoken to him. Others however claim that there is no such man, that the room only ever contains the person who goes into it. Finding himself or herself in the room today the person we are considering realizes that he or she has no other more pressing business to hand and shouts, ‘Is there anyone there?’; ‘If you’re there wise old man, please answer me!’; and perhaps a couple of other similar things, and listens for a reply.

It seems rational—if you’d like to meet this man, but don’t yet believe he exists—to nonetheless give him a shout.

But what if—through no fault of your own—you actively believe there is no wise old man? Here, Mawson says, it still makes sense to call out to him. If he isn’t there, the worst you have done is tried something, and it took less than a minute of your day; if he is there, he might respond, and that would be a very good thing.

The same holds for God. If you don’t believe in God, but want to find out if he does, stubbornly refusing to pray before your credence in theism tips over 50% is probably irrational and anally retentive; in general, if you want to know whether x is the case, it is not a good idea to wall yourself off from a easy source of evidence concerning x.

But if God exists, it stands to reason that many of the billions of people worldwide who think they are in an ongoing relationship with God are in such a relationship, and many of those people think their relationship started through prayer.

If you’re worried about the biasing effects of prayer on your impartial truth-seeking journey (‘If I pray for a few seconds each day, I will lost my Rationality, and my lizard brain will see Krishna’s face in every piece of burnt toast!’ *rips eyebrows*), then just employ a two-pronged strategy of praying, and then trying extra hard to not be irrational (which is an added bonus of Mawson’s challenge, since you should have already been doing that anyway…)

Eyal’s essay takes a different tack—it is about the much-touted secular benefits of prayer; I have nothing especially original to say here, only that the party-line about habitual prayer being healthy seems right, and that it is yet another thing that couldn’t hurt.

I was asked by a long-time-no-see freind at a meeting of the Oxford Socratic Society if I prayed last term, and I replied with something like “less than I should”; although I am not (anymore/yet) a Christian, I still reflexively pray the Lord’s Prayer, which covers all the key bases—thanks, repentance, petition, etc.—without committing to any Christian Doctrines, which is why—for reasons of honesty—I can’t pray the Apostle’s or Nicene Creed.

Sometimes I pray about more specific things; mostly I don’t pray enough.

How should you pray? I don’t know. Probably it helps to pray free-verse on some days, and recite a time-homoured classic on others when you can’t think of what to say. For the atheist who is seeking (reasonable) belief, Mawson recommends the prayer Mark 9:24: “I believe; help my unbelief.”

For something non-Christian (but not anti-Christian), Baháʼís have an oligatory short prayer that I like, which they recite once every 24 hours at noon. In translation it reads,

I bear witness, O my God, that Thou hast created me to know Thee and to worship Thee. I testify, at this moment, to my powerlessness and to Thy might, to my poverty and to Thy wealth. There is none other God but Thee, the Help in Peril, the Self-Subsisting.

Not to sound like an LLM, but this isn’t an abstract philosophical musing—it’s a call to action. Whether or not believe (and in some ways, especially if you don’t believe), you probably have a prudential and epistemic obligation (to yourself, and to your mind), to pray.

item.title: How you, today, can become less of an ideological robot
item.description: the ideological turing test comes to life!
item.content:encoded:
In 2011 coined the ‘Ideological Turing Test’.

In the regular Turing Test, invented by Alan Turing, a human judge chats with a robot. If she can’t tell what she’s interating with—a robot or a person—the robot has passed the test; if the robot gives itself away by its patterns of speech (“That’s not just a good suggestion—it’s a great one!”), it has failed.

In the Ideological Turing Test, you try to convince someone (say, a socialist) that you yourself are a socialist (even though, let’s suppose, you’re not one), in the course of a conversation; ditto for conservatives, libertarians, non-Vegans, Muslims, atheists, techno-optimists, anarcho-capitalists, UFO-ologists, Baptists, and Zionists. Says Caplan, “[t]he ability to pass ideological Turing tests – to state opposing views as clearly and persuasively as their proponents – is a genuine symptom of objectivity and wisdom.”

In other words, if you can’t come off as a True Believer in something you don’t believe, that’s a good sign you haven’t grasped the other side of the case by the nettle to the same extent that you’ve grasped your own. (And, quoting Mill, “[h]e who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that”.) To the extent that you want to master a domain of discourse—when that domain is shot through with controversy—it helps to be able to talk like a respectable member of the Other Side.

Recently my friend Rohan Selva-Radov—a PPE-ist at Merton College, Oxford, whose blog can be found on his website—made One of Us, a free AI tool that lets you do the Ideological Turing Test without any people. One limitation is that you can only test your written words; an ideal test would tell you if you are giving off socialist energy—Maoist facial tics—even if your words are convincingly neoliberal.

Still, the test is pretty great for what it is.

When you click “Start Playing”, the website asks you three questions: (1) where you’d put yourself politically, on a sliding left-to-right scale; (2) an optional question on your age bracket; (3) an optional question on whether you live in the UK, the US, or somewhere else.

You are then assigned an ideology (e.g., centrist), and assigned a short, tweet-length writing task about a political controversy. You type in your centrist-coded response, and the LLM uses its wizardy wordcell powers to see how much you write like a middling moderate.

You might be surprised by the results. E.g., I did poorly as a socialist commenting on a rise in burglaries due to police budget cuts (48/100), but well as an environmentalist tweting about a windfall tax on Shell (86/100). It’s good fun, and I’m curious to see whether my ability to blend in gets better with practice, or whether the only solution is to immerse myself in more opinion journalism so I have a better mental model for how different ideologues tend to write and speak.

(P.S., Let me know in the comments how you find it!)

(P.P.S., And I hope you all had a Merry Christmas [and, more importantly, a happy start to your Kwanzaa festivities🤨])! Apologies for the spotty posting schedule; I’m working on long-ish post about a non-Christian miracle that requires a lot of machine-translation from 19th Century Persian, as well as reading very long and very racist Orientalist histories of Persia. I aim to get that out as soon as possible, but I don’t want to sell you all short on the fact-checking. In the mean time, Tally Ho! I will try dearly to post intermittently in the meantime, especially for my beloved paid subscribers, all of whom I love very much and find very parasocially relatable.)

item.title: Going Awol: 2025 in Review!
item.description: 2025 was a good year for analytic philosophy, the art of writing, and the reading crisis—specifically as it pertains to my newsletter.
item.content:encoded:
2025 was a good year for analytic philosophy, the art of writing, and the reading crisis—specifically as it pertains to my newsletter.

It feels wild to have this many email addresses, surrendered voluntarily, for no reason other than altruism. I mean this—thank you. The number of email marketing agencies I have sold you to is crazy, and I do not plan on stopping.1

Apparently I have published 135 blog posts this year, which surprised me—it felt like substantially less.

In addition, thanks to all of you, my tendrils of influence are spreading all over the globe, although I am less influential than I’d like to be in much of Africa, and Greenland doesn’t seem to care about me at all.

Thanks to father of the blog for WhatsApp-ing an exhaustive list of typo corrections 6-7 minutes after every upload, to and for reasons I am not at liberty to divulge, and to my beautiful paid subscribers, whom I love with every fibre of my immaterial soul.2

I’ve seen a number of people in my feed do this thing where they round up their favourite posts of 2025.

Since it is nearly New Year, and you can only read 2025 articles before the clock strikes twelve, after which the vibe shifts and it becomes bad luck, I will restrict myself to my favourite five.

5.

From my trip to India—feat. rickshaws, vegan food, performative reading, puja, taxis, and a quaint little magic shop.

Special thanks to and for their hospitality, for advice, and to for making it possible.

4.

Because girlfriend of the blog is a Serious Fan, it was important to stand in the pit, meaning there was no water allowed since going to the bathroom meant losing your spot, and there was skant space to read Moral Principles and Political Obligations by A. John Simmons (though I managed to anyway, to the chagrin of other dehydrated/over-heated people who expressed anger that they had to stand up for hours without a classic work of political philosophy to keep them learned.)

3.

I’m chuffed to have established a new sub-field of practical ethics this year, the ethics of cuddling. I thought briefly about submitting to Mind or The Philosophical Review, but my sense is that Substack is now more prestigious now—besides, some advances in moral theory are so important that they deserve to be shared straight away with the public.

2.

For those who are Too Online politically, here is my first and last poem. It features being killed by , being killed by , being killed by himself, being killed by BlueSky, being killed by his grumbling, and so on.

1.

At long last, I came for the Catholics.

This is a genre of article I used to write much more of, and would like to move back into in 2026. In the meantime, see also my impressions of Curtis Yarvin, “philosophy” Substacks, and the young man who started everything, Bentham’s Bulldog.

Finally, if you have requests for the New Year (‘write about pet inerest of mine x’, ‘please, God, not another piece about y’), please let me know in the comments!

And, of course, a very Happy New Year! Thank you for making this year a good one. :)

item.title: Pascal's Wager Without Purple Pixies
item.content:encoded:
Christianity is true. Unfortunately, it’s the 4th century BCE, and the triune God hasn’t taken on flesh and dwelt among us.

Your village has a religious tradition with a good deal of spiritual depth, but, in certain places, your nonsense detector is tingling: they believe in an omnipotent God they call Gashum, but also that rocks are full of purple pixies whose mathematical errors are responsible for earthquakes; every morning, Gashumites pray: “O Gashum! Teach me mathematics, that I may not be like those pixies in rocks, who are assuredly not a spiritual metaphor, who literally cause major earthquakes.”

On the floor of your small wooden hut, you turn through the logic of Pascal’s Wager in your mind: “If I commit to—or virtuously cultivate belief in—whichever religion I take to be most probable, I maximise expected afterlife utility. I can’t force belief, but I could at least assent to a religion I don’t yet believe in, have not-yet-believing faith in its doctrines, pray to its God, etc. But which religion?”

The only other religion you know about belongs to the neighbouring tribe, the Maducees: they believe in an omnipotent God they call Madoun, and that, a hundred and thirty-six years ago, Madoun confered infallibility on a prophet called Steve, instructed him to take a harem of sex slaves, hoard all the food in the village, and force everyone to tell him a bedtime story.

You can’t disprove any of this (historically or philosophically or whatever) but the heuristics you depend on in other contexts to recognise nonsense are barking, and you are confident that, at the end of the day, there are no pixies in rocks, and that Steve is not the real deal.

Assuming you buy into something like Pascal’s Wager, how should you bet in this situation?

My feeling is that an ideally rational Pascalian would not assent to either religion—at least not in full. If an omniscient and morally perfect God exists, and these are the only putative cases of revelation you know of, it’s unlikely that either such revelations are His own; if revelation is coming in this life, it either (i) hasn’t happened yet, or (ii) has happened, but hasn’t reached you geographically.

To pin these “revelations” on God, given the low esteem in which you hold them, would be insulting coming from you, and, living a life of daily, ritualised insult to God is the sort of thing that is likely to tock down your afterlife utility in expectation. (To illustrate, assume expected afterlife utility derives from your relationship with God in the afterlife, and that your closeness to God fixes the value of that relationship, which is partly fixed by the history of that relationship, which is partly fixed by your choices with respect to that relationship. In that case, you might think choosing to pin (what seems to you to be) obvious hokum on the Lord of the Universe over and over would be insulting—the sort of thing that would probably make your future relationship with God less close than it otherwise would have been.)

But even if you think both religions are probably bunkum—taken in their entirety—shouldn’t a Pascalian prefer one of them to nothing at all? It might be that betting on the Gashumite or Maducian faith is a better bet irreligion (stuffing the God-shaped hole in your psychology with popcorn and distraction, never praying, etc.), but it’s not clear to me why either are preferable to praying, reverently contemplating divine things, trying to imitate spiritual exemplars you know, etc., without cashing in to the doctrinal bells and whistles of either religion.

Your best option—in this case—is probably to do the things that the religions around you agree on as being conducive to a relationship with God (e.g., praying a lot, imitating saints, etc.), so long as they don’t seem immoral or insulting (e.g., if both religions said you had to affirm that the sky is green and that murder is good in your devotional practice, it makes sense to leave that practice out, even though the only religious traditions you know about converge on it).

I’m willing to bet that many advocates of Pascal’s Wager who have found their religious home would agree that there have probably been people (before Islam, before Christ) for whom it was best Pascalian practice just to do generic religious things like praying and imitating spiritual exemplars, without converting to the religion on their parents.

But if there have been people who should not have converted to a religion on the basis of Pascal’s Wager (even if they should have fumbled around in the dark and tried their best to lead a religious life), then I think it’s a credible possibility that some people are in that situation now.

In “Why I Am Not A Christian, Muslim, Jew, or Anything Like That”, gives the following analogy for why he has not converted to Christianity, Islam, Judaism, or anything like that:

A Nigerian prince sends you an email, full of spelling and grammatical errors, asking for your bank account details so he can send you $40 million. You know nothing about Nigerian politics or how international bank transfers work, but … come on. This message just looks exactly like what a scammer would say. I don’t know what an actual Nigerian prince would say, but ... not that.

Someone in 2016 said, “Donald Trump is a poor man’s idea of a rich man.” A poor man might think, “If I were rich, I would have gold all over my house. I’d fire people rudely and talk shit to people all the time, ha! And I’d put my name in giant letters on a huge building!” But this is not what actual rich people (other than Trump) are like.

Analogously, the God of the Bible and the Koran is a primitive human’s idea of a great being. It’s what the primitive human imagines he would be like if he had ultimate power. “I’d make everyone worship me! If anyone didn’t want to, I’d torture him. Forever. I’d make my tribe defeat our enemies. And I’d kill the gays, because--gross!”

Humans have recognitional capactities—capacities for quickly sorting the true from the false, the healthy from the unhealthy, the good from the bad, without much cognitive effort. We all, religious and non-religious alike, use them to filter out false religions and cults. I’m sure you’ve dismissed new religious movements without much in the way of research—you’ve just heard something about them (that their prophet recieved an extremely self-serving revelation, that they think mixed-race people are going to hell, or whatever), and thought… “no, this isn’t it,” and moved on.

It’s not hard to imagine that some people are in a similar place with respect to the major world religions.

Given Pascal’s Wager, the stakes are extremely high, and so it may take more evidence to know that a religion is not God’s final revelation than it takes to know that an email is spam; also, religious studies is complicated, and you can’t always believe what you hear about particular relgions—so before passing on all of them and holding out hope for some future religion, it makes sense to look into the religions we already have.

Nevertheless, you might end up judging that the religions you know of look suspiciously like the Gushumite or Maducian faith—spiritually rich in many ways, but also committed to things that look really implausible, to the point where, given how you feel, assenting to one of those religions would be impious and insulting.

For this reason, if your read on religion is similar to Huemer’s, you can still take Pascal’s Wager in a substantive way: by praying, reading time-tested texts that are spiritually rich, thinking about God, repenting of sins, imitating spiritual exemplars, etc., without resignedly converting to Catholicism.

item.title: Two Updates
item.content:encoded:
Hello!

I would like to begin with an apology to my beautiful paid subscribers, whom I love. You see, I have been writing my contribution to the Substack miracle discourse, and it is going to be epic.

This might not sound like a bad thing, as if I were complaining that my cauliflower steak is too juicy, that my girlfriend has an excellent Substack, that my pillow is too plump with loose teeth for the tooth fairy and the wool of several lab grown ewes. However, the downside of writing the yummiest miraclepost of all time is that is has given me a crippling case of writer’s block; all my other blog post ideas feel like straw in comparison, and I hate them.

I intend to spend the next week getting over myself, churning out paid posts at a more acceptable rate, as well as free ones for all you free-loaders. I am sorry for starving you out.

In the meantime, just for today, here are two mini updates.

First, following last week’s blog post that critiqued a paper by Joshua Sijuwade, the veteran blogger, Jesus historian, and radio host kindly offered to set up an in-studio dialogue between Sijuwade and myself on the Unbelievable? radio show! Assuming all goes to plan, the topic is ‘a priori arguments for Christianity’, and it’ll happen later next month.

Second, I did an interview with for his podcast/YouTube Channel! For those of you who have been living under a KETTLE, Miles is a philosopher of religion, Oxford DPhil Student, and owner of a great set of teeth. His YouTube channel is a hidden gem for those who like philosophy of religion and metaethics, and it was a pleasure to appear on his show. In order to bait people’s clicks, Miles and I decided to discuss only topics that are controversial, grabby, and interesting: as a result, should you decide to watch, you will see me steelman the doctrine of eternal hell, defend the Mormon pre-existence theodicy, argue that fine-tuning is empirical evidence for objective beauty, and discuss the miracle evidence for Baháʼí. You consume it on YouTube, Spotify, and Substack.

For a taste of what is to come, WATCH as Miles crumbles like a CRUMBLE and open-mindedly ADMITS, like a LIBERAL, that I raised his credence in aesthetic realism.

item.title: New Blog Announcement! (Baháʼí: An Independent Investigation)
item.description: You only ever hear people talk about their religious investigations in the past tense.
item.content:encoded:
You only ever hear people talk about their religious investigations in the past tense. “I spent months looking into the evidence for Christianity, and was forced to admit that it’s true!”, or, “I spent years looking into Joseph Smith and came to see he’s a fraud!”

Whenever I hear these stories I always think “okay, interesting… I wonder what your investigation looked like, though. What did you read? Was it books or just, like, YouTube comments? What issues did you dig into? How did your thinking evolve over time?”

As some of you know, I have recently been thinking about the Baháʼí faith from an ‘Is this plausible?’ angle. In Baháʼí theology, this is called ‘the Independent Investigation of Reality’, and you are strongly encouraged to do it.

For a bit of context, the Baháʼí faith started in Persia in the early 19th Century, and now has somewhere between 7 and 8 million followers (so: bigger than Jainism, smaller than Judaism.) Its most important religious figure is Baháʼu'lláh, and its central teaching is the unity of Religion, God, and Mankind.

One of Baháʼí’s attractions (besides this) is that it is very pluralistic doctrinally—however, theirs is not an ‘anything goes’ sort of pluralism where you can pick and choose whatever you like and throw it in as you please. In particular, Baháʼís think that nearly all of the major religions derive, historically, from Manifestations of God, each of whom are morally perfect and, in some precise sense that I am still trying to feel out the contours of, theologically infallible. Among these infallible manifestations are the historical Abraham, Moses, Zoroaster, Krishna, Buddha, Jesus, Muhammed, the Báb, and Baha’u’llah.

In some cases, e.g., that of Abraham, Baháʼí is immune from confirmation or falsification: since—I gather—we don’t know much of anything about Abraham’s words or deeds from the perspective of secular history, pointing out a putative example of Abraham acting wrongly, believing falsely, or contradicting another divine manifestation about theology won’t matter much in terms of counter-evidence. By and large, Baháʼís aren’t committed to what manifestations are said to have said and said to have done—just to what they actually said and actually did.

As the ‘manifestations’ move closer to us in time and the written sources move closer in time to theirs (Jesus, Muhammad, etc.) the threat of falsification looms larger: certainly, the bodies of doctrine that sprang from some of these figures are incompatible with Baháʼí theology in places. For example, many Buddhists believe—and believe that the Buddha believed—that there is no persisting immaterial soul that is the seat of personal identity. But since Baháʼís do believe that, it will be a problem, coherence-wise, if the Buddha believed it himself.

Did the historical Buddha teach a metaphysical version no-self view? This is the type of question that an Independent Investigator should be asking. To the extent that there’s evidence of some weight to suggest that he did, there is evidence of some weight against Baháʼí. Unsurprisingly, here is a scholarly debate about how much we can know about what the Buddha thought, including on the no-self question. On my new side-blog, Baháʼí: An Independent Investigation, I will be asking these sorts of questions, live-blogging my reading, credence updates, and conclusions, on the web of beliefs to which the Baháʼí faith is wedded.

Why am I doing this on Substack, out in the open? Good question.

  1. Writing helps me remember things and think stuff through; if I write down what I’m thinking at each stage, I am more likely to think about this stuff well.

  2. If I have to keep posting about what I am reading, I will be incentivised to read like I’m of MIT; if I don’t keep coming out with reading updates, you can justifiably conclude that I am a failure who doesn’t read. Knowing that you will think this of me should spur me to keep reading when intrinsic motivation fails.

  3. This seems like a fun thing to do! There is a lot of material online if you are weighing the evidence for and against Christianity, Islam, or whatever, but not really anything on the Baháʼí religion, and nearly nothing in an analytic theological vein.

  4. If anyone subscribes (I am under no illusions that anybody will subscribe!), they will hopefully tear my provisional conclusions to shreds, question my methods, give me reading recommendations, and generally improve the feng shui of my reflective equilibrium.

“But Amos”, you weep, crying bitterly, “why are you doing this on a separate side-blog, and what does this mean for subscribers of Going Awol?” Good question. Basically: I’m keeping this stuff (mostly) on another blog because I intend to get really boring and into the weeds about things like the history of the Babi movement and the teachings of Shoghi Effendi, and most of you did not subscribe for such things.

As for what it means for Going Awol addicts, not much: I will still blog here, using this venue for more interesting and entertaining stuff—stuff for your amusement and amazement. Having a side-blog where I can nerd out more freely will, I hope, loosen my writer’s block by getting the less entertaining garbage out of my system, which is often what I want to write about first.

Much of the stuff on the new blog will be paywalled: this is because I will be writing about a religion that I am not an expert on, whose members are very persecuted, and whose teachings are not widely understood, and I don’t want to spread religious confusion to the masses or take public stances when I’m not ready to. However: if you are already a paid subscriber to Going Awol and want to follow along with my private religious investigations, shoot me your email address via Substack DMs and I will give you a gift subscription (this is so that on the off chance that I do post here less, you will still be getting something for your money.)

Also, if you are some sort of expert on Baháʼí/Bábí studies (or on something that I go on to rabbit-hole) let me know, and I will also give you a freebie, since I want you to have the option of commenting and steering me right. And some posts will of course be free.

In any case, since I don’t want to money-grub too much about religious truth-seeking, paid subscriptions will be pretty cheap: $5 a month or $50 a year.

What will I write about? Who knows! But probably all sorts of things—Jesus’ apocalypticism, Twelver Shi’ism, past statements of the Universal House of Justice, scholarly catfights between Denis MacEoin and Baháʼí historians, the Miracle of the Bab, hadith criticism, Baháʼí metaphysics, and whatever I deem to be relevant. Posts might consist of me summarizing books and papers I’ve read, dissecting quotes, posing weird objections, stress-testing arguments, and doing whatever I deem to be on-topic.

If that interests you, subscribe here! If not, no worries: I will still be posting over here, flooding your inbox with Beauty, Truth, and Goodness.

P.S., if that really interests you and you want to read other writing on here about Baháʼí stuff, I know that —Identity theft is not a joke, Jim! Millions of families suffer every year!—blogs about it sometimes at . (See also his interview with , which was great.) In the comments of my interview with Baháʼí philosopher Joshua Hall, mentioned that he had a Substack called the about the Baháʼí writings and philosophy, including some of his own provisional translations of Bahá’u’lláh. I especially recommend this blog. If anyone knows of any others, drop their names in the comments!

item.title: Links for March
item.content:encoded:
1. The infamous v debate on the Miracle of the Sun at Fatima is now available, courtesy of . More than anything, the debate was a triumph of the human spirit. When I argue with Ethan, I struggle to stay afloat on topics that I have researched for days and which Ethan has never heard of before; yet Dustin, powered by several hours of Wikipedia research and a couple of blog posts, was able to keep up the fight for almost two hours on a topic that Ethan knows more about that nearly anyone else on the planet. Dustin’s most formidable debate tactic, which he tells me is not a tactic, is to involuntarily chuckle and then casually repeat what his opponent said back to them in a way that makes it sound like the dumbest thing that has ever been said by anyone. He also employs the counter-signal, whereby he drops all pretentions and academic verbiage, thereby revealing that he doesn’t need them. Ethan’s style is to methodically and articulately say why you are wrong, interweaving ‘clear appeals to common sense that any ordinary person can understand’ with the fact that he actually corresponded with the author of the study you’re appealing to, searched his bins, hacked into his mind, memorized all of his prior work on the embryology of dinosaur embryos, and found two-hundred and fifty independently converging lines of evidence that the work is an academic fraud whose data, interpreted correctly, actually supports Ethan’s contention about how “Augustine” ought to be pronounced. It’s a worthwhile debate even if you don’t care about cool and interesting miracle reports that are obviously cool and interesting; for rhetorical lessons alone, I think there is a lot to be gleaned from it.

  2. I really like this normative ethics paper by Sacha Arridge, “Morality demands more of you the better you are”. Insanely good people often believe that their insanely good actions are morally required of them, even though nearly everyone else would think their actions go above and beyond what morality requires. One solution is to say that the heroes are wrong, and the moral normies are right; another is to say that the heroes are right, and the moral normies are wrong. Sacha’s solution is to say that morality demands more of you the more virtuous you are. That way, a moral hero who rushes into a burning building to save two children can be right that what they did was required, and we lesser beings can be right that morality wouldn’t demand such heroism of us.

  3. My in-studio debate with Josh Sijuwade is now available on YouTube and Spotify! Our host was the inestimable of , and the topic was a priori arguments for Christianity. (In particular, Josh has a priori arguments for the Trinity and the Incarnation, which am not convinced by.) Having interacted with Josh, my conclusion is that he is a stand up guy, and I am pleased with how it went, especially the second half, which was on Josh’s argument for the Trinity. My only concern is that the audience might have trouble following all the argumentative moves, given the time constraints we were under.

  4. One of the topics that came up was ‘omnisubjectivity’, the divine attribute whereby God knows what it’s like to be a bat. If that tickles your interest, there was a recent symposium in the new philosophy of religion journal Agatheos on omnisubjectivity and whether it makes sense. All of the papers are open access, and you can read them by clicking this link.

  5. Watch me pull a tic tac from my eyeball.

  6. Cool coincidence: in the 19th century, a powder-keg for millenarian religious movements, the largest millenarian movement in the Christian world—the Millerites—and the largest millenarian movement in the Islamic world—Shaykhism—both independently converged on the year 1844 as the year we would receive the return of an old prophet (for the Millerites, Jesus Christ, for the Imami Twelvers, the Twelfth Imam). (Well, sort of. The Millerites predicted that Christ would return within the window of March 21, 1843, and March 21, 1844; still, pretty neat, given that both groups got the 1844 number from different places—the Millerites, from William Miller’s mathematical interpretation of Daniel 8; the Shaykhis, by counting 1000 lunar years from when the Twelfth Imam went into occultation.)

  7. Brian Cutter (author of a paper arguing that substance dualists should have at least a middling credence that future AIs will be ensouled) debates Bálint Békefi (author of a response paper, arguing that we should doubt this) on the YouTube Channel, hosted by . (Watch here.)

  8. In 1984, Alvin Plantinga published a famous essay called “Advice to Christian Philosophers.” Since then, periodically, Christian philosophers have written follow-ups in an attempt to update his advice for each generation. Last year, Christian B. Miller, Meghan Sullivan, Devin Gouvêa, Gregory Robson, Matthew Frise, and Philip Swenson put out “Advice to Christian Philosophers, Forty Years Later”; last month, Ryan Mullins put out a podcast called “Advice to Young Christian Philosophers”. I suspect both will be relevant to people in my audience who want to do work in philosophy of religion, Christian and non-Christian both.

  9. Andreas Mogensen has an interesting argument for why, even if AIs aren’t conscious, they might still be welfare subjects (as in, things can be good or bad for them in a morally relevant sense). Basically, if we’re somewhat sympathetic to desire satisfaction accounts of wellbeing (on which your life goes better for you to the extent that your desires are satisfied, and worse for you to the extent that your desires are frustrated), and we take seriously the idea that there can be unconscious desires (e.g., Martin Luther King’s desire for justice, which he has even while he is sleeping), then we should be open to the idea that AI systems literally have desires that can be frustrated or satisfied, making them welfare subjects. You’ve probably already thought of an objection, and I, too, suspect that the argument breaks down; still, I am not entirely sure why it breaks down, and I encourage you to read the paper, since it is very careful, and it almost certainly addresses your objection.

  10. Not a fan of desire satisfaction theories? Your work isn’t done. Mogensen has another paper, where he does the same thing for objective list theories.

  11. If you’re driving today, here is a longform podcast with Mogensen where he breaks down the arguments, and then talks about negative utilitarianism.

  12. From the same podcasters (80,000 hours): mirror bacteria is terrifying, and we should all be freaking out about it.

  13. A paper on why successful religions are more likely to be true.

  14. A paper on the doctrine of divine simplicity.

  15. , hosted by Troy Dana, is the best analytic philosophy channel on YouTube. He’s interviewed a boatload of analytic philosophers on everything from philosophy of fiction to decision theory to God to time to everything under the sun. Recently, in a fit of benevolence, he dumped all of his past episodes on Spotify!

  16. There is a new book out from Oxford University Press called The Nature of Belief, edited by Johnathan Lewis-Jong and ; the whole thing is open access, and it looks fantastic.

  17. debates two proponents of Advaita Vedanta Hinduism; wins.

  18. Tim Mawson debates Asha Lancaster-Thomas on pantheism; wins.

  19. and on whether philosophy is a waste of time.

  20. Would you still love me if I were a worm?

  21. In a paywalled post, I argued that the only plausible conception of eternal hell is one where life in hell is net-positive, but worse than life in heaven. A new paper by Martin Lembke makes a similar argument, bringing in a bunch of historical stuff I had no idea about. (Did you know that in 1884 there was an article called “Happiness in Hell” defending this position that got put on the Vatican’s index of prohibited reading?)

item.title: How to solve the problem of political obligation
item.description: in defence of the gratitude theory
item.content:encoded:
[epistemic status: idk]

Once upon a time, in Dutyville, Dublin, Coilín O’Connor was cleaning his pot of gold, which he had found at the end of a rainbow.

His television box, powered by potato peel, was relating the six o’clock news. So I was speaking to the Government of Ireland so I was. And they said to me, so they said, ‘We’re imposing a pot of gold tax, so we are!’

Coilín knew how to avoid a pot of gold tax. He could simply bury it at the foot of a rainbow, mark the spot with a clover, and roll up the rainbow so no one would ever come looking for it.

But in Dutyville, Dublin, people care about doing their duty. If there is no free-standing moral duty to obey the law, Coilín will want to hide his riches; if there is a moral duty to obey the law, Coilín will want to pay what he owes.

I.

The problem of political obligation is the problem of pinning down why—if at all—Coilín has a moral duty to obey the law, even if we can get away with breaking it.

Philosophical anarchists are radicals who think there are no political obligations. You have no duty to follow the law, just because it came from the government. (Of course, you have a moral duty to, e.g., obey the law against murder, but that’s just because murder is independently wrong, and the criminal law happens to recognise that. If an Act of Parliament brought The Purge to life, it would still be wrong to participate.)

is the most famous philosophical anarchist on Substack. In The Problem of Political Authority: An Examination of the Right to Coerce and the Duty to Obey, Huemer argues both that the state is illegitimate (i.e., it has no right to coerce us, through taxes, regulations, etc., except when it’s an emergency), and that political obligation is fake and illusory.

Political legitimacy and political obligation come apart; you can believe in one and doubt the other. Alternatively, you can believe in both (and be a political normie), or believe in neither (and be a philosophical anarchist).1

One theory of political obligation that gets almost no romantic attention is the gratitude theory, which models the duty to obey the law after the duty to buy flowers for the person who saved you from an alligator. Basically, the idea is that, in a relatively just state, most people are significantly benefited by their government, and this gives us a presumptive—if overridable—duty to submit to the law.

In The Right and the Good, old-timey Oxford philosopher W.D. Ross expressed sympathy for this idea: “…the duty of obeying the laws of one’s country arises partly (as Socrates contends in the Crito) from the duty of gratitude for the benefits one has received from it”2. And A.C. Ewing, an old-timey Cambridge philosopher, wrote that “[t]he obligation to one’s country or state is more analogous to the obligations to our parents than it is to a business relation. Here also the debt is not incurred deliberately […] and here also it seems to depend, mainly at least, on uncovenanted benefits conferred on us.”3

My guess is, these days, there is a widespread feeling that the gratitude theory was decisively put to bed in 1979 by A. John Simmons. In An Instrumentalist Theory of Political Legitimacy, Matthias Brinkman exhorts readers to “…follow the Simmons rule: for any proposed explanation of authority, one needs to look up the relevant part of John Simmons’s extensive philosophical work over many decades where he has refuted the attempt.”4

Simmons treated the gratitude theory at the end of his 1979 classic, Moral Principles and Political Obligations. Since then, support for the gratitude theory has sort of fizzled. One guy, A.D.M. Walker, defended the view in the late 1990s, and Richard Swinburne has pledged his allegiance to it across a number of books and papers (most recently, Could a Good God Permit So Much Suffering: A Debate), but only briefly, and in a philosophy of religion context that no political philosophers will hear about. Apart from that, the theory has only a small fistful of defenders, who defend it in the narrow context of whether refugees have a duty to be grateful to the countries that take them in.

When I read Moral Principles and Political Obligations at a Lana Del Rey concert, I was underwhelmed by Simmons’s reply to the gratitude theory. “Can this be it?”, I wondered, as Mrs. Del Rey (Del Dufrene?) sung about why you should stand by your man even when he is hard to understand. “But I do understand him”, I thought to myself, “and his refutation of the gratitude theory isn’t hitting!”

Today I will steelman the gratitude theory of political obligation against nearly every criticism in the political philosophy literature I’m aware of. At times, I’ll make moves I’m not really sure about, and act much more confident than I am or should be. This is all part of the process, and if you do not like it, you are invited to take it up with the chief of police.

Subscribe now

II.

The gratitude theory of political obligation (of the sort I want to defend), says that typically, citizens of a reasonably just state have an unchosen obligation of gratitude to the government, in virtue of what it’s done for them vis-à-vis safety, economic prosperity, justice before the law, healthcare, and so on.

To the extent that your government has been failing in these respects, your obligation of gratitude is diminished; to the extent that it’s completely screwed you over and ruined your life, you probably don’t owe them anything.

And this obligation of gratitude, if it binds you, gives you a pro tanto reason to obey the law, since this is how the government—qua institution—wants that obligation to be discharged.

In many cases, the duty to follow the law for reasons of gratitude might not be super strong, and overrideable in lots of cases; some may find this feature of the view objectionable, but intuitively, to my mind, that is exactly how it should be—if there is a legal duty to rat out one’s friend over a minor infraction, only the Red Forman’s and Stan Smiths of the world think your all-things-considered obligation would be to inform the police of his crimes.

III.

Here are some objections people have to the gratitude theory.

Objection #1: When a benefactor is morally obligated to confer a benefit, duties of gratitude don’t arise; but the government is morally obligated to keep us safe, provide healthcare, etc., so we have no debt of gratitude to the government when it does those things.

Reply: I reject the starting premise. If I get hit by a car and you find me lying on the road, you are morally obligated to help me if it’s at minimal cost to yourself; but, if you do help me, I clearly still have a duty of gratitude.

Objection #2: The government, as a whole, makes no special sacrifice—or if it does, very little—when it benefits you in particular; but you only owe a debt of gratitude when your benefactor made some serious, special sacrifice in an effort to benefit your.

Reply: I deny that you don’t owe a debt of gratitude when no serious, special sacrifice was made to benefit you in particular. If you found me drowning and all you had to do was toss a small rubber ring like it was the easiest thing in the world, I think I still incur an obligation of gratitude.

Objection #3: You only have a duty of gratitude if you’re (meaningfully) able to reject the benefits you receive. But it’s extremely hard to avoid receiving any benefits from your government. To avoid the security it provides, you might need to flee your country for a War Zone, or the South Pole. So, you have no debt of gratitude to the government.

Reply #3: You can incur duties of gratitude for benefits that you could not have rejected—in fact, such duties are extremely widespread. If someone carries you in their womb for nine months, for example, you do have an obligation of gratitude to that person, even though, because you were so little, you had very little say in the matter.

Objection #4: Sometimes the government majorly screws over its citizens—e.g., confines them to life in a slum, subjects them to apartheid, imprisons them unjustly, etc. So, the gratitude theory is the only theory we employ, won’t that mean that some people don’t have a duty to obey the law in cases where it harms no one, when they won’t get caught, etc.

Reply #4: Yes, and this is the right result. If the government fails to keep you safe, routinely disrespects you, spits in your face, steals your house, shoots your dog, etc., and then tells you not to smoke a menthol cigarette in the privacy of your own home where the only victim of your behaviour is you, it’s not intuitive—to me, at least—that you have any non-self-protective reason to obey that law. The duty to obey is something that states must earn—they don’t just get it for free.

Objection #5: Even if we owe a duty of gratitude to the state, duties of gratitude can be fulfilled in all kinds of ways, by conferring all kinds of benefits on one’s benefactor. One way to pay back the state might be to do what they tell me (within reason), but another way might be to, e.g., write influential blog posts against philosophical anarchist, spreading awareness about all the good things the government does for us, etc.5

Reply: Suppose you bake me a scrumptious vegan cake when I’m poorly that totally makes my week, and I incur a duty of gratitude. At that stage, I could discharge my debt of gratitude in multiple different ways: by writing a thank you note, making you vegan cupcakes, etc.

But suppose I’m the considerate type, and I ask you, “What can I do for you?” You are British about it at first and say “no no, I don’t want anything”, but I insist, and eventually you crack and ask me to share some of my vegan biscuits that I have lying next to me. Once you say that, my duty to benefit in some generic way hardens into a duty to benefit you in this, very precise way.

Suppose, now, I don’t ask out loud what I can do for you, but I know ahead of time that if I asked that question, you would 100% ask for some of my biscuits. In that case, I think, I have a perfect duty to benefit you precisely my sharing by biscuits, not in some other way.

In the case of the government, I am nearly certain that if I sent a letter to my head of state, or asked a question of parliament, or whatever, whether they would rather I obey all their laws or disobey some of their laws (in particular, the laws that it wouldn’t be independently immoral to violate, like those against jaywalking) but benefit them in some other way, like writing really influential blog posts that help to rekindle faith in government, the official position of the government, qua group, would be that they want me to obey the law.

(This is true, I claim, even if each politician would privately prefer that I break the law and write my influential, pro-government blog posts; as I’ll argue in the next reply, the political obligation of gratitude is owed to the government, not the individuals who make it up. Consequently, it’s what the government wants, qua collective body, that matters, not what individual political actors want. And group desires are not reducible to the aggregate desires of group members.)

Objection #6: Duties of gratitude only arise when your benefactor benefits you intentionally. But governments are groups, and groups can’t literally ‘intend’ things.6

Reply #6: I agree that duties of gratitude only arise when benefits are conferred intentionally; to take an example from Simmons, suppose you’re being mugged, but I inadvertently save you by walking by, scaring off the mugger with my big, hulking frame. In that case, even if you’re grateful that I walked by, you don’t incur a duty of gratitude.

What I disagree with (at least in my persona as devil’s advocate), is the implausible, unmotivated, reductionist view that groups don’t literally have motives and intentions that are irreducible to the motives and intentions of individuals.

There is a ginormous and very boring academic literature on collective intentionally and anti-reductionist approaches thereto. To spare you some of that, here is one-paragraph statement of the case from Timothy Williamson:

“[A]scriptions of intentional action or intention to a collective subject are arguably irreducible to ascriptions of intentional action or intention to its members. When the selection committee intends to offer the job to a given candidate, nothing much follows about the intentions of its members, who may negligently fail to form any appropriate intentions, or treacherously form intentions to subvert the committee’s decision.”

The committee example is a good one. Suppose a selection committee unanimously votes to hire you, starting Friday; in that case, it seems true that the committee intends to hire you, starting Friday.

But suppose, privately, each individual committee member belonged to a different Millenarian sect, such that they all believed, with alarming certainty, that Christ would return on Thursday and rapture us all into Heaven. As a result, no individual member of the board intends, with the others, to hire you on Friday; even still, the committee intends to hire you on Friday.

Applied to the government: even in cases where every politician is a devious so-and-so who is only in it for himself, the government can—qua group—literally intend to benefit you, in a manner that is irreducible to the intentions of the politicians and civil servants who comprise it.

(A related objection might be that groups—like governments—do no literally have benevolent motives. I find it hard to respond to this objection in a concise way because there is no general agreement on what a ‘motive’ is; but presumably, it has something to do with a agent’s desires, beliefs, and intentions. I won’t go into it here, but there are similar anti-reductionist arguments for irreducible group desires (“What do we want? Climate justice!”) and irreducible group beliefs, in addition to irreducible group intentions. So whatever a ‘motive’ is, the defender of this objection has their work cut out for them if they want to lean on this objection.

IV.

As it happens, I think there are at least two pretty decent objections to the gratitude theory, and for that reason I’m reluctant to accept it. Unfortunately, I will have to leave in in suspense, because it is time to vacate the library.

My parting message is just that the gratitude theory of political obligation is underrated; the reasons it’s normally rejected on the basis of are lame, and we should all be more grateful that its here.

E.g., I might have standing to demand you to apologise, giving you a duty to apologise, but lack the standing to threaten you with violence if you refuse to do so. (You might ask, but isn’t ‘government’ by definition the monopoly on coercion within a given geographical area? Perhaps, but in theory you could have a government

item.title: Cope in philosophy of religion
item.description: The internet has a useful bit of of verbiage that I think more philosophers of religion—and philosophers in general—should use more often.
item.content:encoded:
The internet has a useful bit of of verbiage that I think philosophers of religion—and philosophers in general—should use more often.

The sense of “cope” I have in mind is related to this, but a bit different, insofar as it’s non-pejorative.

Suppose Bob can’t see a way out of being Catholic because he thinks the miracle evidence for it is borderline epistemically coercive: he examines the evidence for the Miracle of the Sun at Fatima, eucharistic miracles, the healings at Lourdes, the apparitions at Zeitoun, Padre Pio’s stigmata’s, the levitations of St. Joseph of Cupertino, etc., thinks, “shoot, I don’t really see any plausible non-Catholic explanations that are as plausible as the unified Catholic explanation”, and so signs up for an RCIA class.

Some people on Substack might be facing this problem right now.

On converting, however, there are a lot of magisterial teachings Bob will have to assent to that, independent of his commitment to Catholicism, he would’ve found very hard to believe (if I were Bob, some of these might include belief in eternal hell, the belief that early abortion is wrong, the belief that contraception wrong, the belief that lying is categorically wrong—i.e., wrong even to avert the apocalypse1—, the doctrine of divine simplicity, religious particularism, the trinity, the atonement, etc.)

One way of dealing with the cognitive dissonance would be to lose your mind and convince yourself that these beliefs that don’t appear to sit well with your evidence are actually super plausible and obvious. E.g., Bob could pretend that Thomistic natural law theory is clearly, on its own merits, the most plausible ethical theory, and that the Church’s teaching on contraception is basically just follows from Common Sense.

A different route is to lean fully into the mystery and not even hazard a guess as to why these claims that you find so implausible are true. “It’s a complete mystery why God allows people to languish in Hell forever—I have literally no idea why He does this, and I refuse to guess!” This will work for some people, and in some cases, it might even be the right thing to do.

However, some people are too pathologically curious to not even hazard a guess as to why the things they’re committed to are true, so this won’t work for them.

The last option, the one I think more people should be comfortable fessing up to, is to cope, and cope with total transparency. By this, I mean: looking for, and tentatively endorsing, what you take to be the least-worst-but-still-implausible way to rescue your view, while being open that that’s what you’re doing.

To take a related example, totally out of the blue, take the doctrine of the Trinity, according to which God is tripersonal.

Let’s be so for real: there is no compelling argument for the claim that a perfect being would have to be triune, in the way that there is a compelling argument for why a perfect being would have to be morally good. So, this seems like a clear case where Christianity will have to take a bit of a probabilistic hit: the doctrine of the trinity adds extra complexity to Christianity’s fundamental ontology, giving it a lower prior probability than unitarian monotheism.

A number of smart people in Christian history have felt the force of this worry, and so have tried to come up with a priori arguments for why a perfect being would have to be exactly tri-personal (as opposed to di-personal or quad-personal.) I recently had a friendly debate with the Christian philosopher Joshua Sijuwade, where we talked about his a priori argument for the trinity, which centres on God’s love of Himself:

Subscribe now

Suffice it to say, I don’t think any a priori argument for the trinity has what it takes to actually persuade anyone. A better framing for these sorts of arguments, I think, is that they are—at their best—a form of virtuous cope. Trinitarianism puts pressure on the Christian philosopher to venture their least-worst guess as to why God would be tri-personal; the guess doesn’t have to be convertible into an argument that should, by itself, persuade anyone to believe in the trinity. It just has to lighten the load of being a trinitarian a bit, by showing that there is some not-completely-absurd story about why God would be triune.2

Read as cope, the tradition of Christian philosophers trying to lighten their load by coming up with a priori reasons makes more sense, and is easier to justify.

‘Cope’ is not a dirty word. There are cases where everyone would admit that coping is completely rational. Suppose, to take ’s example, the entire text of the Qur’an was coded into the initial conditions of the Big Bang in perfect Arabic, such that when you gazed up at the stars, or peered down the lens of a microscope, you could read, clear as day, “Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds: Merciful to all, Compassionate to each!”, etc. Suppose you knew you weren’t hallucinating, because all the other scientists could see it too.3

In this case, it seems like the reasonable thing is probably to believe in some form of Islam.

But now suppose an Unbeliever confronts you with a piece of evidence against Islam that you don’t think is easily dismissed. For example, suppose they convince you, against the view of some scholars, that the right interpretation of Surah 4:157 is that it’s denying that Jesus died by crucifixion—but, they insist, our best historical evidence suggests that Jesus did die by crucifixion, and so there is historical evidence against Islam.

One option would be to (dishonestly, given your credences) pretend that you find their argument less pressing than you actually find it; another option is to refuse to look for an answer; but a third—and more rational—option, would be to openly cope, and endorse, in full transparency, the least-worst solution you can think of, while admitting that, on the merits, it is not an independently plausible solution (for example, maybe the verse is actually saying that they didn’t successfully kill Jesus in the spiritual sense that his soul lived on, even though, to you, it doesn’t really look like the verse is saying that.)

To admit that you’re endorsing the least-worst-but-still-implausible solution to a problem for Islam isn’t to admit that Islam is false or that the majority of your evidence tells against it; remember, the stars literally spell out the Qur’an! All you’re doing is coping—and that is the right thing to do, so long as you are up front about it.

When I think about a topic, I try to keep a mental list of which bits I think are actually plausible on the merits, and the bits I accept because of cope. Doing this (explicitly calling it ‘cope’) has the effect of reducing intellectual self-deception, and shattering the temptations of pretentiousness.

If I’ve explicitly called a part of my view “cope”—especially out loud, in conversation with someone else—it is much harder to turn around and trick myself that every part of my view is plausible on the merits, and much easier to remember the list of problems with my view when it comes time to re-weigh the pros and cons.
